meta.title: The Root Ladder
meta.summary: The five forms are not five alternatives but consecutive, interlocking windows in the fixed order C-A-G-E-D, sharing six roots between them.

spans.text: Five forms, five lessons, and it can look like five separate ways to play the same chord. It isn't. Laid end to end, the five forms are one continuous ladder of windows climbing the neck, and every root you've met so far is a rung on it.

You already saw the seam at the top of this ladder: the D form's upper root,
, is the same note as the C form's upper root,
, an octave up. Fret 12 is where the pattern comes back around, so the ladder doesn't run out at the D form — it wraps, and the C form starts over exactly where the D form left off.
Here is the concrete version of the same claim, and it's the strongest fact in this chapter: there are only six
s in the first twelve frets, and every one of them except the very first belongs to two forms at once.
The forms are not five sets of different notes. They are five overlapping views of one set of six roots, and the overlap is the whole reason the neck feels continuous once you can see it this way.

You will not be asked to learn a new shape after this chapter. Chapters 2, 3 and 4 put more notes inside these same five windows — first the third and fifth, then the major pentatonic, then the whole major scale. The windows don't change. Only how much of each one is lit.
